name: Battle of the Little Bighorn
note: A schematic plan. The accounts do not give a map of the field: the village, the small hill, the ford and Custer's route are placed to suit the story, and the precise route of Custer's battalion and the north end of the village remain disputed. Custer's own movements are shown by one account among several.

phases.title: Reno crosses the river and charges the village
phases.text: Reno's three troops forded the Little Bighorn at the mouth of Reno Creek on Custer's orders and rode towards the village. Custer's battalion followed the ridges to the east, while Benteen and the pack train were still behind.
phases.quote: Reno's force crossed the Little Bighorn at the mouth of what is today Reno Creek around 3:10 pm on June 25.

phases.title: Reno dismounts and the warriors ride out
phases.text: Reno stopped a few hundred yards short of the village, fearing a trap, and put his men into a skirmish line. The mounted warriors streamed out and rode against the centre and exposed left end of the line.
phases.quote: He ordered his troopers to dismount and deploy in a skirmish line, according to standard army doctrine.

phases.title: The warriors turn Reno's left and he falls back to the trees
phases.text: Over 500 warriors massed behind a small hill on Reno's left and attacked his left and rear. Reno withdrew into the timber along the river bend, where the warriors pinned his men down.
phases.quote: From this position the Indians mounted an attack of more than 500 warriors against the left and rear of Reno's line, turning Reno's exposed left flank.

phases.title: Reno's men break for the bluffs
phases.text: Reno led his men out of the timber in a disorderly rout along the river. They crossed under attack and climbed the bluffs on the far side, leaving wounded behind in the timber.
phases.quote: Abandoning the wounded, he led a disorderly rout for a mile next to the river.

phases.title: Benteen and the pack train join Reno on the bluffs
phases.text: Benteen's three troops reached Reno's shaken men while they were still climbing from the valley, and McDougall's troop and the pack train came later. The command dug rifle pits and held an all-round defence.
phases.quote: Reno's depleted and shaken troops were joined by Captain Benteen's column

phases.title: Weir's troops advance to Weir Peaks
phases.text: Captain Weir and Company D moved out to contact Custer, and troops D, M and K advanced a mile north to Weir Peaks and dismounted. From there Weir could see the size of the camps and warriors moving about in the distance.
phases.quote: D, M and K advanced a mile to what is today Weir Peaks or Weir Point, and dismounted.

phases.title: Weir's troops are attacked and fall back to Reno Hill
phases.text: The three troops on Weir Peaks were attacked by warriors, who increasingly came from the finished fight with Custer. On Reno's order they withdrew, and all seven companies fell back to Reno Hill.
phases.quote: The three troops (D, M, K) which had dismounted and remained at Weir Peaks (RCOI figure 9) were soon attacked by native hostiles

phases.title: Yates' companies appear at the mouth of Medicine Tail Coulee
phases.text: With Reno driven from the village, Custer moved north and a wing of his battalion under Yates went down to the river at the Minneconjou Ford. Hundreds of warriors left the fight with Reno to protect the village.
phases.quote: caused hundreds of warriors to disengage from the Reno valley fight and return to deal with the threat to the village

phases.title: Custer's battalion is overwhelmed on Custer Hill
phases.text: Custer's companies moved to Custer Hill, where the warriors, led by Crazy Horse by the Lakota account, charged from the northeast. Custer's remaining troops, E, F and half of C, were soon killed.
phases.quote: Custer's remaining troops (E, F, and half of C) were soon killed.
